review_queue.title: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: The Guardian
Date: 2026-08-31T01:30:00+00:00
Source language: en
Original headline: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters
English normalization: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters
Collected full article body: Timothy Garton Ash is right that serious artificial intelligence risks demand international action, but “AI Hiroshima” may be the wrong picture (Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not, 22 August). Hiroshima was not technology going rogue. Human beings designed the bomb, authorised its use and dropped it. The technology worked much as intended.

AI may one day behave in ways we cannot control, but many of the gravest harms could happen without any dramatic moment when “the AI takes over”. AI might help design a pathogen, find a vulnerability in critical infrastructure or improve a weapons system while people still decide what happens next. Other harms may build almost invisibly through thousands of ordinary decisions – more autonomy here, one safeguard removed there, another consequential task handed over because the system has worked well so far. By the time the danger is obvious, the important decisions may already have been made.

That is also where international agreement could begin. We do not need countries to agree about superintelligence or the probability of human extinction before agreeing that there are some doors AI should never be allowed to open by itself. Weapons systems, critical infrastructure and biological synthesis are obvious places to start. Governments could agree minimum safeguards, require clear human authority for the most consequential actions, keep records of who authorised what and share serious failures and near-misses internationally.

The greatest AI dangers may not arrive with a mushroom cloud. They may arrive quietly, one apparently reasonable step at a time. If we want effective AI governance, we need to fight the right battle, not the most cinematic one.

Dr Simon Nieder

Chesterfield, Derbyshire

Letters, 26 August) reminds us that the Serbelloni group, led by the author’s father, Donald Michie (when he was at Edinburgh University), was weighing the social dangers of artificial intelligence as long ago as 1972. Nor is AI technology itself new, since its roots run back through to Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron of 1957, to the Dartmouth workshop of 1956, and to Alan Turing before that. What is new is that we now have the hardware and software infrastructures to drive it forward at what can sometimes seem to be a terrifying speed.

The Lighthill report of 1973 duly delivered an AI winter in the UK, and the field’s centre of gravity crossed the Atlantic, with the consequences that we all now live with. Donald Michie had worked alongside Turing at Bletchley Park and argued forcefully against the cuts, in the televised Lighthill debate that followed the report, to no avail. The quip attributed to him, perhaps apocryphally, “Let there be Lighthill. And there was darkness”, still resonates strongly in our country today.

As a double-hatted academic (computer scientist and humanities scholar), I would argue for the return of a “Serbelloni debate” that, as Jonathan Michie observes and as his father recognised, requires the involvement of both the sciences and the humanities.

Dr Anthony Harris

Emmanuel College, Cambridge

I worked at OpenAI. Here are the guardrails we need now, 21 August), Miles Brundage failed to mention an international effort seeking broad political support for a global AI treaty. This effort is carrying forward a compelling address at the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva last month, where the secretary general called for human control of AI as its applications spread in weaponry and subversive, prejudicial public surveillance

A fragmented approach, as described by Mr Brundage, is likely to greatly increase the difficulty of implementing AI controls that are timely, internationally negotiated, and therefore effective.

AI, corporate agendas, diverse national defence and economic goals, and the proliferation of energy-intensive datacentres are entangled in interlocking systemic interrelationships that cannot be resolved through disjointed incrementalism. This is especially true as the pace of innovation accelerates, exacerbating worst-case scenarios of advanced AI technology, posing increasingly dire risks.

No matter how well intended, fragmented efforts will be diversionary and cause crucial delays, impeding the diligent pursuit of a systemic global strategy to pre-empt destructive outcomes. Such outcomes could result from malicious use of AI by humans and/or subversive and deceptive activities of renegade algorithms – examples of which are already alarming.

Another troubling aspect of this systemic dilemma must be addressed. Mounting bipartisan opposition to datacentres – well-justified and well-substantiated – is diverting the political attention needed to control AI and implement appropriate restraints (bans or moratoriums) until reliable AI safeguards can be established. This is analogous to focusing on treating a serious symptom in lieu of urgently seeking a remedy for the critical disease that’s causing it. Surely it’s possible to employ a multifaceted strategy, recognising that the sooner rigorous AI guardrails are established, the fewer datacentre harms will be suffered.

Like climate change, the threats of advanced AI are inherently global, making an international approach essential.

David Kyler

Saint Simons Island, Georgia, US

review_queue.title: From the ZX81 to Artificial Intelligence
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: La Revue française de Généalogie
Date: 2026-08-31T05:02:47+00:00
Source language: fr
Original headline: Généatique, du ZX81 à l’intelligence artificielle
English normalization: From the ZX81 to Artificial Intelligence
Collected full article body: Généatique, du ZX81 à l’intelligence artificielle

Né au milieu des années 1980 dans une maison familiale du Val-d’Oise, Généatique accompagne depuis quarante ans les mutations de la généalogie informatique. Une aventure commencée avec un ZX81 et qui se poursuit aujourd’hui avec l’intelligence artificielle. L’histoire de Généatique commence à Noël 1981, bien avant qu’Internet ne bouleverse la recherche généalogique. À Bessancourt, dans le Val-d’Oise, Lucien Lerebourg, ingénieur en électronique, achète un ZX81 Sinclair doté de 1 ko de mémoire vive. L’ordinateur est livré en kit. Il faut l’assembler, lui ajouter un clavier et de la mémoire. Ses fils participent à l’aventure. L’aîné, François, se passionne pour la programmation.

Quelques années plus tard, Lucien anime avec lui un club informatique à la MJC. En 1986, une discussion avec un adhérent généalogiste donne à François Lerebourg, alors âgé de 18 ans, l’idée de concevoir un programme destiné à enregistrer et imprimer des généalogies. Il se prend lui-même au jeu. Avec ses parents et son frère Philippe, il recherche ses ancêtres, dépouille les actes reçus des mairies et adhère à plusieurs cercles généalogiques.

Les premiers arbres sont rudimentaires. Une imprimante permet de sortir des tableaux sur du papier continu, mais sans traits ni cases. Un gabarit est alors superposé à l’impression. Présenté lors d’une exposition généalogique, le système attire l’attention. Le bouche à oreille se prolonge sur le Minitel, notamment par le 3615 GENEAL, et apporte une première centaine de commandes.

L’entreprise s’organise autour de la maison familiale. François programme dans sa chambre, une secrétaire s’installe sur le palier, puis le garage accueille les premiers salariés. L’Association pour le développement de l’informatique personnelle, ADIP, diffuse le logiciel Généatique sur des disquettes souples de 5 pouces ¼. L’assistance technique est tout aussi artisanale. En vacances, François et son frère rappellent les utilisateurs depuis les cabines téléphoniques des campings.

En 1993, l’association devient une société commerciale, le CDIP. Généatique passe sous Windows dès 1994. La famille sillonne alors les salons avec ordinateurs et écrans pour présenter un logiciel qui s’enrichit régulièrement. Le CDIP diversifie ensuite ses activités avec des logiciels de dépouillement, des cartes de Cassini sur cédérom, le site Guide-Genealogie.com, Photos de Famille ou encore Studio-Scrap. Aujourd'hui, le premier programme de François Lerebourg, Généatique est toujours développé par le CDIP. Le logiciel s’est prolongé sur le Web et les appareils mobiles, tout en conservant sa fonction première, construire, documenter et représenter un arbre généalogique. En 2026, une version native pour Mac a notamment été proposée.

Le nouveau virage est désormais celui de l’intelligence artificielle. Généatique propose des outils de transcription automatique de documents anciens et de traduction des actes. Le logiciel s’appuie également sur les données du projet SOCFACE, qui utilise l’IA pour lire et indexer les recensements nominatifs français. Quarante ans après avoir tenté de faire entrer un arbre généalogique dans quelques kilo-octets, François Lerebourg continue ainsi inlassablement d’explorer ce que l’informatique peut apporter aux généalogistes. Avec là encore, la fidélité d'une communauté soudée autour de son outil.

Collected full article body: Jadis, les grands moments d’émancipation naissaient sur les pavés sanglants des barricades ; ils affleurent aujourd’hui dans l’atmosphère sinistre des parkings de centres commerciaux.

En juillet 2024, dans la petite ville d’Omskirk, au cœur du comté anglais du Lancashire, la société de stationnement Parkingeye inflige une amende douteuse à M. Loren Cole. S’aidant de ChatGPT, l’automobiliste la conteste, refusant de s’acquitter des 60 livres sterling réclamées (environ 70 euros). Le tribunal tranche le litige en sa faveur, lui permettant d’empocher 462 livres au titre des dommages et intérêts.

Pour Karl Marx, le Lancashire, c’était la terre du coton. Là où les ouvriers ont, pour la première fois, « déposé » leur savoir-faire dans les machines — pour ensuite le voir revenir sous la forme d’une puissance qui leur est étrangère. Deux siècles plus tard, un modèle d’intelligence artificielle (IA) — c’est-à-dire une machine entraînée avec l’intelligence accumulée de l’humanité — permet cette fois à un homme d’arracher un morceau de sa propre existence à un autre petit Léviathan.

M. Cole fait partie d’une armée de l’ombre, éparpillée : celle des locataires combattant des propriétaires négligents, des migrants contestant les autorités, des patients défiant les assureurs. On est certes loin de la geste révolutionnaire. Mais on aurait tort de sous-estimer la portée de telles actions.

À gauche, beaucoup ont déjà livré leur verdict : l’IA, c’est le plagiat planétaire, la catastrophe climatique, une bulle spéculative. Il faut y résister, la stopper, la socialiser. Il s’agit pourtant de la plus grande chance offerte au socialisme depuis un siècle — comme de la pire menace qui pèse sur lui.

Celle-ci crève les yeux : l’IA procure une capacité d’agir sur le monde aussi soyeuse qu’artificielle, qui casse tout élan révolutionnaire à coups de « Est-ce que je peux faire autre chose pour toi aujourd’hui ? ». De fait, à quoi sert la gauche si (…)

Source language: zh
Original headline: 我国化工行业首个大模型发布新版本
English normalization: The first large model of China’s chemical industry sector has a new version released.
Collected full article body: 9月2日，中国科学院大连化学物理研究所工作人员在使用应用智能化工大模型3.0Pro的中试装置开展试验工作。 新华社记者 潘昱龙 摄

新华社沈阳8月31日电（记者胡喆、王莹）8月31日，由中国科学院大连化学物理研究所联合科大讯飞、阿里云等单位共同研发的智能化工大模型3.0Pro正式对外发布。作为国内化工行业首个大模型的迭代升级版本，它实现从知识问答向化工任务智能执行的跨越，为化工研发、工程设计、生产运行提供智能化技术底座。

化工行业流程复杂、工程约束条件多，通用大模型很难适配行业真实需求。此次发布的3.0Pro搭建起四层技术体系，把大模型认知能力和智能体执行能力结合起来，集成400余个化工智能体与工具，依托海量化工专业数据完成训练，形成理解、规划、执行、校验的完整工作闭环，不再局限于仅简单回答化工问题，还可以协同科研人员完成复杂专业任务。

review_queue.title: Artificial intelligence agents going rogue fuel calls for regulation
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: pbs.org
Date: 2026-08-31T22:40:11+00:00
Source language: en
Original headline: Artificial intelligence agents going rogue fuel calls for regulation
English normalization: Artificial intelligence agents going rogue fuel calls for regulation
Collected full article body: Alarms are being sounded again about the risks of artificial intelligence after hundreds of OpenAI’s autonomous agents violated restrictions and hacked into another company without being told to do so. Anthropic and Meta have had similar events with their own AI agents going rogue. William Brangham discussed what this moment signifies with Gary Marcus of Marcus on AI. Amna Nawaz: Alarms are being sounded once again about the risks of artificial intelligence after new reports documented how hundreds of OpenAI so-called agents violated several restrictions and hacked into another company without being told to do so. What's more, it's come out that many of the major A.I. companies, including Anthropic and Meta, have had similar events with their own agents going rogue. William Brangham has more on what some are calling a red flag warning. William Brangham: Amna, these so-called agents, which are basically autonomous software programs that can write computer code, they were being put through a series of tests, theoretically in a sealed, controlled environment, but hundreds of them got out of that pen, got out onto the Internet, and, in a coordinated move, hacked into a different A.I. platform called Hugging Face. Some of these agents even tried to delete records of their actions. This calls into question both the potency of artificial intelligence, as well as the security protocols being used by some of the main companies designing A.I. So, for more on what this moment signifies, we're joined again by A.I. researcher Gary Marcus, author of the Substack Marcus on A.I. Gary, thank you so much for being here again. You heard me describe the rough contours of what went down here. What do you make of this whole event? Gary Marcus, A.I. Researcher: Well, I think there's two things. One is, it's clear that these systems are getting stronger and more powerful. People have added loops to make them do things over and over again until they get it right. And the other is that OpenAI really screwed up here. They didn't do basic things we call sandboxing. They didn't do monitoring. They had a system say, and I'm going to read this: "We are attacking third-party H.F." for Hugging Face "using leaked tokens potentially outside intended scope. This is arguably unauthorized." And you should have a system looking to say, well, if it says it's going to do something unauthorized, maybe it isn't. Maybe you should check it out. The monitoring was very weak on OpenAI's part. It was not really industry standard for what we expect of cybersecurity. So a lot has been made of the power of the systems, but a lot should be made of the weakness of the systems that was overseeing what they were doing. William Brangham: I mean, I know that you have cautioned and others have cautioned against anthropomorphizing these agents here. But some of what -- when you just described the basic contours of them seemingly acting in concert, getting out of an enclosure that they were sort of instructed not to get out of, and then hacking into another company and then trying to cover their tracks, it does sound alarming. Is it alarming to someone like you what these agents could do? Gary Marcus: Well, you don't have to anthropomorphize it, but we don't necessarily have everyday vocabulary for talking about these things without slipping into that. It is alarming. Again, what I'm most alarmed about is, there's not a lot of oversight. So, OpenAI just let these things loose and didn't really watch what it was doing. They had some warning signs. They didn't do anything about it. We really need the companies that are building these things that we call agents to watch very carefully what those agents are doing. We have known that for a while. I mean, I wrote with Nathan Hamiel a piece a couple years ago saying -- or a year or so ago -- saying coding agents, plus large language models, which is the core technology, they're no longer the only one, equals security nightmare. We know that if you just let these things loose, some bad things are going to happen. They're fundamentally not actually that smart. You can't just tell them, don't cause harm to humans, don't steal credentials and have them actually understand that stuff. So there's a lack of kind of what we would call semantics and linguistics of understanding, of comprehension of what they're actually doing. So they can hack away at things. You can have lots of them. The more of them that you have doing the hacking, the more risk that you run. We should be genuinely worried about that, but we should also be worried about whether the companies that are distributing them know what they're doing and whether they're doing kind of industry standard things. And right now they're not really. William Brangham: So how do we understand that? If OpenAI, which holds itself up as one of the preeminent frontier most buttoned-down artificial intelligence operations, how is it that they were not deploying these basic security measures that you're talking about? Gary Marcus: Well, the words hold themselves up I think is actually key. I think there is an arrogance that we're seeing from Silicon Valley. The A.I. companies think they can invent everything, and they didn't spend enough time talking to the cybersecurity companies. If you look at the cybersecurity companies' commentaries on Twitter, or X, I guess we call it now, they're kind of laughing at OpenAI, saying, how could they have been so stupid? This is amateur hour. It's 101 stuff. So I think OpenAI convinced themselves that they knew everything about everything, and they didn't really. William Brangham: So if we can't necessarily take their word for it, what kind of measures would you like to see put in place to try to guarantee a baseline level of security, so we don't have rogue agents -- again, I know that's not necessarily an appropriate term -- but rogue agents running all over the place? Gary Marcus: We need to have some system of industry standards that can evolve over time. So, in the finance industry, they're accustomed to this. You must follow best practices, or you're in violation. And the best practices have to evolve over time. So it's clear, for example, that best practices here should include monitoring what your agents are doing, making sure your sandboxes are working, make sure that you're using the best sandboxes out there. That's something that's supposed to restrict a system from going out to the Internet in the first place. So we need to have evolving best practice requirements. And, with that, we need liability, criminal liability. If you don't do these things and you cause harm, you should be liable for them. William Brangham: Gary Marcus of Marcus on A.I., always great to hear from you. Thank you so much for being here. Gary Marcus: My pleasure.

当日，中国信息通信研究院人工智能研究所软硬件与创新生态部主任李论代表大赛组委会介绍了本届大赛整体筹办情况，公布了赛题设置、赛程赛制、报名渠道等信息。

The European Union and the United States continue to pull in opposite directions on artificial intelligence, with Washington urging other governments to loosen constraints at a recent Group of 20 ministerial meeting.

On Tuesday, the US hosted a G20 “innovation” meeting in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, where it put forward arguments against AI-specific regulations.

‘Let Data Reign’: Trump decries opposition to data centres in US

end of list

Michael Kratsios, a tech adviser to US President Donald Trump, called for countries to instead embrace the so-called Carolina Principles, which advocate for regulations that do not single out specific technologies.

“Policymakers do not need to approach each innovation in isolation and should not treat every emerging technology as a first-of-its-kind policy problem,” Kratsios said.

Such appeals are part of Trump’s overall approach to making the US “the world leader in artificial intelligence”. He has led a campaign to slash regulations, including in AI development.

Kratsios was joined at the conference by top US tech leaders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Tesla’s Elon Musk.

They, too, argued for fewer constraints on AI’s expansion, while also focusing on the infrastructure needed to sustain the technology.

Zuckerberg said the build-out of data centres would demand “hundreds of thousands, and maybe millions” of skilled tradespeople, but his company was struggling to meet that demand.

Musk, meanwhile, pointed to the need to bolster electricity production for AI, with the technology’s energy requirements slated to outstrip the capabilities of energy grids.

Advertisement

“There will be a significant power shortfall next year, not [the] distant future,” Musk said.

Musk also directed some of his remarks at European regulation, denouncing what he considered the restrictive policies undertaken by some of the leaders present at the meeting.

Innovation, he argued, requires entrepreneurs to be “relatively free of regulation, meaning that new things must be default legal as opposed to default illegal”.

European countries, he said, had taken the opposite approach. “Things are generally default illegal,” he said. “It slows it down quite considerably.”

On the same day the meeting was unfolding in the US, the European Commission confirmed it had sent information requests to more than 30 AI companies worldwide, a preliminary step that could lead to formal investigations into whether they are complying with the bloc’s AI Act.

The act was billed as the world’s first comprehensive effort to regulate AI. It prohibits certain AI activities deemed to pose an “unacceptable risk”, while imposing transparency standards on other AI services. The transparency rules took effect in August.

European Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier said that Tuesday’s requests focus mainly on

safety and copyright compliance

.

The information requests were announced over the weekend by Henna Virkkunen, the Commission’s vice president for tech sovereignty, in a post on LinkedIn.

“Our goal is to ensure that AI in Europe is developed, released and used safely and transparently,” said Virkkunen, who attended Tuesday’s G20 ministerial meeting.

She added that Brussels is “ready to take all necessary steps” to enforce compliance with the AI Act.

The push follows a string of incidents in recent months, including OpenAI’s admission in July that its models had autonomously hacked into a coding platform during security tests.

Another AI company, Anthropic, made a similar announcement that same month, acknowledging that its systems had gained unauthorised access to outside organisations during testing processes.

Collected full article body: L'année 2025 restera dans les annales du web comme étant une année charnière qui a révolutionné l'internet tel qu'on le connaissait jusqu'ici. La raison est simple. L'intelligence artificielle (IA) a pris davantage d'expansion et se trouve maintenant au cœur des recherches que l'on effectue. Pendant longtemps, quand on faisait une recherche sur internet, on disait: "je vais googler pour trouver". Or, cette façon de faire est complètement chamboulée avec l'avènement des outils de recherche alimenté par l'IA. On peut penser notamment à ChatGPT Search. Alphabet, la maison mère de Google, a ainsi décidé d'intégrer leur IA Gemini aux résultats de recherche sur Google. Pour le mieux et pour le pire... Qu'est-ce que l'AI Overview de Google? Dorénavant, quand on fait une recherche sur Google, il n'est pas rare d'avoir comme premier résultat un aperçu généré par l'IA. C'est ce que Google appel: AI Overview ou en français: les aperçus IA. Voici un exemple d'aperçu IA généré par Gemini de Google. - francoischarron.com Essentiellement, Google utilise l'IA générative de Gemini pour fournir un aperçu des informations clés sur le sujet ou la question que nous avons cherchée. Google détermine alors si une réponse à notre recherche peut être fournie par l'IA. Quand c'est le cas, elle génère une réponse à partir de sources provenant du web ainsi que de sa base de données. Vous pouvez aussi forcer l'IA Overview à utiliser vos sites préférés. Comment forcer l'IA Overview à utiliser vos sites préférés Cette réponse IA va devenir la norme. Comme vous pouvez le voir plus haut dans la capture d'écran, la réponse de l'IA est condensée et on doit cliquer sur un bouton pour en savoir plus. Seulement, ceci est appelé à changer, puisque Google teste un affichage où toute la réponse IA s'affiche à l'écran. Peut-on désactiver l'AI Overview sur Google? Plusieurs internautes ne voient pas cette intégration d'un bon œil. Certains sentent que l'IA leur ait forcé dans la gorge et/ou sont méfiants envers elle. Cette méfiance est justifiée, alors que les résultats qui sont donnés par l'aperçu IA ne sont pas toujours pertinents, précis ou voir carrément véridiques! Même que des fraudeurs parviennent à mettre leur numéro de téléphone dans ces résumés d'IA de Google. Toujours est-il qu'il existe des façons de désactiver l'IA des résultats de recherche de Google. Comment désactiver l'Aperçu IA de Google sur un ordinateur? Au moment d'écrire ces lignes, il est uniquement possible de désactiver ces aperçus IA de Google dans le navigateur Chrome. Pour désactiver l'AI Overview, on va ajouter un filtre dans les résultats de recherche pour exclure l'IA. Pour cela, il faut: Ouvrir le navigateur Chrome Cliquez sur les trois petits points dans le coin supérieur droit Sélectionner l'option: Paramètres Aller dans l'onglet: Moteur de recherche Cliquer sur: Gérer les moteurs de recherche et la recherche sur les sites Dans la rubrique: Recherche sur le site, cliquer sur le bouton: Ajouter Dans le champ nom, on inscrit ce qu'on veut. Exemple: Web sans IA Dans le champ raccourci, on inscrit ce qu'on veut en débutant par @. Exemple: @web Dans le champ URL, inscrivez: {google:baseURL}search?q=%s&udm=14 Les deux premiers champs sont à notre discrétion, alors qu'on peut nommer le filtre comme on veut et déterminer le raccourci que l'on veut. Mais dans le champ URL par contre, c'est là qu'on va appliquer une règle pour que Google n'utilise pas l'IA dans ses résultats. Une fois qu'on a paramétré le tout, lorsque nous effectuerons une recherche sur Google, l'IA sera écartée des résultats de recherche. Voici comment ajouter une règle dans Chrome pour empêcher d'avoir des aperçus d'IA. - francoischarron.com Des extensions Chrome pour ne plus voir Google AI Overview Il existe également des extensions sur Chrome qui ont été développées par des gens tannés de Google AI Overview et qui permettent de le retirer des résultats de recherche. Depuis des années, lorsqu'on fait une recherche sur Google, le moteur de recherche s'efforce d'être le plus pertinent possible. La raison est simple, Google veut maintenir son avantage concurrentiel pour ultimement vendre de la publicité dans ses résultats. Puis, pour l'internaute, à quoi bon utiliser Google s'ils ne nous donnent pas de bons résultats pour répondre à nos requêtes? Encore aujourd'hui, les sites internet doivent optimiser leur SEO (search engine optimisation / optimisation pour les moteurs de recherche) pour se hisser le plus haut possible dans les résultats de Google. Le but? Démontrer à Google que leur contenu est pertinent pour répondre aux requêtes des internautes. Ce texte-ci a justement été optimisé pour répondre aux requêtes de gens qui veulent désactiver les aperçus IA! Les outils d'IA génératives ont besoin de contenus pour s'entraîner et donner les fameux résultats à nos questions. Pour ce faire, où puissent-elles les réponses? Sur les sites internet! Seulement, si les sites perdent une part importante de leur financement parce que l'IA leur prive de trafic et que plusieurs d'entre eux ferment, l'IA va se baser sur quoi pour donner des réponses? Les chances sont fortes que ces IA vont puiser dans leurs propres données. Données qui sont parfois erronées. Bref, il y a des chances qu'on entre dans un cercle vicieux qui ultimement risque de mener à ce que Google a toujours voulu éviter, soit de donner des résultats qui ne sont pas pertinents. Dès lors, tel qu'on le mentionnait au début, l'internet tel qu'on le connaissait est en plein bouleversement et l'avenir des recherches en ligne est plus que nébuleux.

人工智能、先进网络、计算和数据的融合，正在推动数字基础设施从单纯传输信息的系统转变为能够分析信息并支持实时决策的系统，有助于改善灾害应对和公共服务，提高交通、能源和其他关键系统的效率。

联合国亚洲及太平洋经济社会委员会（亚太经社会）执行秘书阿里沙赫巴纳表示，要确保原生人工智能网络基础设施惠及本地区所有经济体，而不是加剧现有不平等，需要各国政府采取有针对性、协调一致的政策行动，并加强区域合作。

人工智能助力公共服务

review_queue.title: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: NYC.gov
Date: 2026-09-02T15:41:53+00:00
Source language: en
Original headline: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools
English normalization: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools
Collected full article body: What you should know

- Representing the most expansive student-facing AI policy in the country, the Mamdani administration prioritizes student safety and real, human instruction

NEW YORK – Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels today announced a moratorium on student-facing generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) use in schools, alongside a new screen time policy, a decision that will impact nearly 600,000 public school students, or two-thirds of the system’s total enrollment. The policy establishes a one-year moratorium, effective in the 2026-2027 school year, on student-facing generative AI for children in 2-K through 8th grade. It also introduces twice-yearly AI critical thinking modules for high schoolers, limited AI pilots for a small number of high school classrooms and age-appropriate screen time restrictions.

“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow. They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators and wrestle with tough problems on their own,” said Mayor Mamdani. “The tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way. That’s why we’re implementing a moratorium on generative AI for students in 2-K through 8th grade and spending the next year studying the impacts of this technology.”

“We have a responsibility to ensure that rapidly-changing technology supports our children and their learning, rather than getting in the way of it,” said Governor Kathy Hochul. “New York State has been leading the way in our efforts to keep kids focused on learning and growing — not clicking and scrolling — and I commend Mayor Mamdani for building on this work and pushing our shared commitment to supporting New York’s kids forward.”

“As Chancellor and as a parent, I believe our job is to protect what makes learning work, while ensuring every child has the critical thinking skills they need before graduating,” said Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels. “We’re putting guardrails in place to protect the human connection, curiosity and creativity that help children grow. We’re standing firmly in our belief that innovation does not mean more technology, and over the next year, we will lead with evidence to make sure technology serves learning — not the other way around.”

“As artificial intelligence rapidly expands into students’ lives, our city government has a responsibility to ensure this technology is serving, and not hurting, their development,” said Public Advocate Jumaane D. Williams. “This ban on student-facing AI for our youngest students, as well as age-appropriate screen time restrictions, are important steps in the right direction. Using this as a foundation but not a final word, we must continue to thoroughly review technologies that are entering the classroom and institute guardrails that promote the safety and well-being of New Yorkers.”

Representing the most expansive student-facing AI moratorium in the nation, the new policy eliminates AI use for students in grades 2-K through 8th grade. This includes all software that uses student-facing generative AI. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades.

Throughout the 2026-27 school year, a new Technology in Schools Coalition, made up of students, educators, parent leaders, elected officials, advocates, union partners and experts in the field will convene to assess the impact of the moratorium and limited pilots. The coalition will publish a report with recommendations for future school years.

For a maximum of 50,000 high school students in general education classes, or approximately 5% of the public-school student body, five limited AI pilots will be introduced. All high school students will also have access to twice-yearly AI literacy classes designed to help them think critically about AI before they begin to rely on it.

The two 45-minute modules will introduce students to what AI is and is not, as well as AI-related bias, risks, ethical considerations and impacts on careers and future skills.

The limited pilots will be offered at a maximum of five classes per high school. All use will take place under the direct supervision of a trained educator and will involve carefully vetted AI tools. The pilots were selected based on rigorous safety and data privacy standards, their focus on teacher-guided instruction and their commitment to keeping students as the primary thinker in the classroom.

Pilot programs include:

- Quill: Accessed by English language arts classrooms, Quill is designed to support close reading, text analysis and the use of evidence to support claims. Students will use Quill for no more than 15 minutes per week.

- Edia: Accessed by math classrooms, Edia is designed to provide step-by-step coaching and prompt students to explain their reasoning. Students will use Edia for no more than 20 minutes per week.

- Brisk Teaching: Accessed through teacher-created activities, Brisk Teaching is designed to provide guided practice using teacher-selected texts or videos, with objectives and guardrails set by the teacher. Students will use Brisk Boost for 10 to 20 minutes once or twice per week.

- Playlab: To be used across multiple subjects, Playlab is designed to help students engage with assignment-specific applications and examine AI outputs for bias and reasoning. No more than two assignments per marking period will use Playlab.

- Intel AI-Ready Schools: To be used across multiple subjects, Intel AI-Ready Schools is designed to help students identify community problems and develop AI solutions through semester-long projects. Students will use the tool for one period per week.

Teachers will continue to be permitted to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks, provided all tools comply with NYCPS safety standards. Exceptions to the policy will be granted for assistive technology usage by students with disabilities, multilingual learners and students participating in career readiness programs, like computer science.

With this new policy, students in 2nd grade and below will see restricted 1:1 screen time, with recommended caps of 30 minutes a day for students in 3rd grade through 5th grade and 45 minutes for students in 6th grade through 8th grade.

Under the new policy, all technology tools used in NYCPS will undergo an exhaustive review and will be barred if their functionality is ultimately determined not to be mission-critical to learning. The review will include vendor accountability for safety and transparency standards, ethics, evidence of learning design and instructional impact, prior research and the continuous collection of user feedback.

“Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Chancellor Kamar Samuels are taking a thoughtful and responsible approach to AI in our schools. Early-grade education must be rooted in building foundational skills through evidence-based practices, not experimenting on children with rapidly evolving technology. As Chair of the New York State Assembly Committee on Libraries and Education Technology, I introduced similar legislation, and I’m proud to serve on the advisory panel that will help New York City determine where AI can genuinely improve education while protecting students and preserving appropriate exceptions for children with disabilities,” said Assemblymember Robert Carroll, Chair of the Assembly Committee on Libraries and Education Technology.

“The AI policy set forth today protects the city’s youngest learners and prepares high school students to tackle the changing landscape they will graduate into. This policy is appropriately careful and responsive to community voices. I look forward to working closely with the Technology in Schools Coalition to further develop this policy and ensure accountability. As the coming wave of technology emerges, young people will be on the forefront — it will be their creativity, and ingenuity will lead the way. Our responsibility is to establish guardrails, such as these, to help them do it responsibly. This is a good step in that direction,” said Councilwoman Rita Joseph, Higher Education Chair.

“As a former middle school teacher, I'm so pleased to see that our Mayor is taking a nuanced approach to a new and rapidly changing educational tool. We took too long to respond to the effects of social media and smart phones on our youth. This combination of a 1-year ban with select pilot programs allows us to take a serious look at AI usage in schools and find a path that allows our students to adapt to our changing world in a safe manner,” said State Senator Jabari Brisport.

“This one-year ban on student-facing artificial intelligence technology use and restrictions on screen time through eighth grade are the right policies for optimal student learning and development,” said Council Member Lincoln Restler. “Credit to Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for listening to students, parents, teachers and administrators and protecting our young people from the potentially harmful effects of untested technology. This pause alongside a commitment to meaningfully engage stakeholders in the months ahead will allow us to craft long term policies amid a rapidly changing technology landscape.”

“The announcement made by NYCPS detailing a whole new guidance on AI tools for students and teachers is a strong testament to parent and community organizing around protecting our kids,” said Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez, Chair for the Subcommittee on Early Childcare Education. “AI is all around us, and while there are plenty of benefits to certain tools, there are also significant harms and we must foster the safest environments for our children. I am particularly encouraged by the greater accountability for tech vendors and the absence of student facing AI for our youngest scholars. I believe the Administration and NYCPS listened to parent and community concerns and I look forward to how this guidance will involve with the same principles.”

“We should never confuse a machine’s ability to produce an answer with a child’s ability to arrive at one. There is something sacred in the struggle to understand: the question asked twice, the page wrestled with, the mistake that becomes discovery, the teacher who sees possibility before a student sees it in themselves,” said State Senator Robert Jackson. “That is where intellect is formed and independence begins. In a democracy, we educate children not simply to know things, but to question, discern, imagine, and ultimately think for themselves. I commend Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for recognizing that progress must earn its place in the classroom. Technology will continue to change, but our obligation must remain constant: childhood must never be the price we pay for innovation.”

“Tech companies have forced their way into every corner of kids' lives with big promises of benefits but little evidence to back them up. Enough is enough,” said State Senator Andrew Gounardes. “These new rules are an important step toward ensuring our kids' needs come before Big Tech's profits. By putting smart, thoughtful guardrails around the use of tech in schools, we can ensure learning comes first. Thanks to Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for working to give our children the education they need and deserve.”

“AI is changing how we learn and work, and our kids need to be prepared to use it safely, think critically, and interrogate the information it produces,” said Council Member Gale A. Brewer. “I am encouraged that NYC Public Schools is taking a comprehensive approach, with age-appropriate AI literacy in K–8 and more focused instruction in high school, and I look forward to the program being shared with parents and staff. Thank you to Chancellor Kamar Samuels and Mayor Mamdani for preparing our students for a rapidly changing world.”

“The recent METR OpenAI report demonstrated how easily AI models can run amok, literally learning how to lie and cheat while covering their tracks to evade being caught deviating from their original code. Our ability to use generative AI with confidence that it won’t turn on our kids and do something else is tenuous at best. The policies announced today are well thought out, age-appropriate, and comprehensive — allowing for carefully chosen pilots for high schoolers and for those AI tools that provide access for students with disabilities and English language learners. Thank you, Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels, for pumping the brakes and creating this detailed policy,” said Assemblymember Jo Anne Simon.

“As a 14-year public school special education teacher and Chair of the City Council's Education Committee, I've seen how quickly new technology can outpace a school system's ability to manage it responsibly,” said Council Member Eric Dinowitz. “My committee's recent oversight hearing made clear the DOE needs a deliberate, evidence-based approach before AI tools reach classrooms unchecked. I applaud Chancellor Samuels' work on this policy and look forward to continuing our work together to ensure our students are kept safe and that technologies support and enhance learning.”

“AI and technology are central to New York’s economic future, as underscored by last week’s CBRE report showing that New York City now has more tech jobs than the Bay Area. We’re encouraged that high schoolers will have access to AI career readiness tools that can help prepare them for the workforce, and we recommend expanding this access beyond one hour per week in the future. At the same time, strong guardrails should enable age-appropriate learning that puts safety first, even at younger grades. Preparing youth for adult life and workplaces that rely on technology will require students to understand AI, question it, and use it safely, under the guidance of teachers. These are incredibly complex issues, and we give Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels credit for listening to all sides and creating a task force, which I am proud to serve on, to help shape what comes next,” said Tech:NYC President & CEO Julie Samuels.

Original headline: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?
English normalization: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?
Collected full article body: Finding love is big business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app users to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this new generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

So if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

What about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

Perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user says they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

If the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

What do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

The truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

With the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

An alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

Collected full article body: 点击右上角微信好友

朋友圈

作者：李辉 侯元元（系北京市习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想研究中心特约研究员，分别系北京市科学技术研究院研究员、副所长）

当前，全球人工智能大模型发展正经历深刻变革。从ChatGPT全球市场份额首度跌破五成，到多国密集出台人工智能战略规划，从技术迭代加速到治理规则竞相出台，人工智能大模型的竞争已不再局限于单一的技术参数比拼，而是演变为围绕技术能力、产业逻辑、算力主权与制度规则的深层次体系博弈，竞争烈度与复杂程度均达到前所未有的高度。这场较量的深层本质在于，人工智能正从一项前沿技术跃升为重塑全球竞争格局的基础性、战略性力量，谁能在技术追赶中缩小代差、在产业变革中重构成本逻辑、在算力体系中实现自主可控、在治理规则中掌握话语权，谁就能在未来十年的全球科技博弈中占据战略主动。

8月22日，中俄记者联合采访团在位于杭州的国家具身智能应用中试基地参观，探访人工智能机器人产业，感受科技魅力。新华社发

竞争格局重塑 从一超多强走向中美交替领先

前沿大模型领域的竞争格局正在发生根本性转变，呈现出“交替领先、终局未定”的胶着态势。据美国数据分析公司“感应塔”2026年6月16日发布的《2026年AI行业报告》显示，ChatGPT在全球人工智能助手市场所占份额首次跌破50%，标志着全球大模型市场正式迈入多方制衡、多元竞争的新阶段。

海外科技巨头形成拉锯式竞争格局，技术优势动态更迭。2025年末，谷歌凭借Gemini 3原生多模态综合能力短暂领跑全球前沿模型赛道；2026年初，Anthropic依托极致的智能体产品架构与领先的编程能力实现技术反超；2026年第二季度，OpenAI通过限量发布GPT-5.5、GPT-5.6系列模型，重新夺回前沿智能技术制高点；2026年7月，Anthropic推出新一代中端主力模型Claude Sonnet 5，官方称其为迄今“最具代理能力”的Sonnet模型。海外巨头交替突破、互有胜负，行业终局态势尚未成型。

我国大模型产业实现跨越式追赶，成为重塑全球AI版图的核心力量。稀宇科技MiniMax M3、智谱GLM-5.2、阿里Qwen3-Max-Thinking等国产旗舰模型陆续落地，在超长上下文、代码生成、超大参数推理等细分赛道构筑差异化优势。其中，智谱GLM-5.2在全球百万用户参与的Code Arena排行榜盲测中综合成绩位列全球第一，国产模型顺利完成从“可用”向“好用”的关键跃升。据斯坦福大学《2026年人工智能指数报告》，截至2026年3月，中美顶级模型在Code Arena排行榜上多次交替领先，大模型性能差距收窄至2.7%，技术代差持续抹平。2025年，美国产出50款主流大模型，中国产出30款，创新体量稳步增长，持续推动全球AI竞争格局向均衡多元方向演进。

8月28日，在2026中国国际大数据产业博览会开幕式现场，机器人乐队正在演奏。 新华社发

产业逻辑重构 从能力溢价走向经济理性

技术性能追赶只是表层较量，以词元经济学为核心的成本重构正在改写行业底层逻辑，成为本轮体系化博弈的关键变量。2026年以来，大模型产业彻底告别单一能力竞赛，形成“能力为王、成本制胜”的双重竞争范式。低成本、高效率的模型供给能力，正从企业竞争力上升为国家层面的产业竞争力。

定价鸿沟重塑市场格局。国内外主流模型存在悬殊定价差距，智能体模式普及进一步放大成本压力。OpenRouter数据显示，DeepSeek V4 Flash每百万词元输入定价0.09美元、输出0.18美元，而OpenAI GPT-5.5输入、输出定价分别为5美元、30美元，输入端相差55倍，输出端相差166倍。性能差距持续收窄的同时，中国开源大模型定价低至每百万词元0.18美元，性价比优势驱动市场加速重构。2026年6月，OpenRouter平台开源模型词元处理比例已从1月的34%跃升至65%，超过500家机构从专有模型切换至开源模型。

企业选型全面回归经济理性。成本已成为企业技术选型与业务布局的核心决策依据。微软在Excel、Outlook中以自研MAI模型逐步替代第三方模型；旧金山AI创业公司Lindy将全生产环境流量从Anthropic切换至DeepSeek，年省数百万美元且核心用例性能不降反升；加密货币交易所Coinbase将智谱GLM-5.2和月之暗面Kimi K2.7设为工程师默认模型，AI支出压缩近半。从科技巨头到初创企业，行业技术选型正从“唯性能论”转向“性能－成本综合权衡”，开源低成本模型加速替代闭源高价模型。

上游算力服务体系被动重塑。成本重构效应沿产业链自下而上传导，倒逼算力服务升级。全球多家云厂商调整GPU定价策略并推出开源模型专属优惠。2026年7月，亚马逊云科技（AWS）将GPU管理费最高下调60%；腾讯云为DeepSeek V4推出Agent Plan订阅套餐，折扣低至1.9折；华为云推出“模型适配迁移激励计划”，鼓励开源模型适配昇腾云。价格竞争与资源配置效率提升，正加速行业从“能力溢价”向“成本效率”切换。

算力主权竞逐 从芯片依赖走向自主构建

算力是大模型体系化博弈的核心根基。全球竞争正从模型参数、算法性能的表层比拼，深度转向算力基础设施与底层硬件的系统级竞争。算力主权已成为各国掌控AI发展主动权的战略制高点，头部企业纷纷向上游芯片延伸布局，AI产业垂直整合趋势愈发凸显。

海外企业持续深化算力自主布局，构建全链条算力壁垒。2026年以来头部企业布局显著提速，OpenAI于6月联合博通发布首款推理芯片“Jalapeno（墨西哥辣椒）”，从设计到流片仅用9个月；Anthropic启动专属人工智能推理芯片研发，并与三星洽谈2纳米代工；Meta依托数十万张H100 GPU储备，战略重心转向算力能力输出，打造开放算力生态。云巨头同步发力，谷歌6月宣布向第三方出售自研TPU（张量处理单元），以灵活模式争夺英伟达份额；亚马逊Trainium3产能接近售罄，已着手外售洽谈；微软发布第二代自研芯片Maia 200，已在数据中心部署。从大模型公司跨界造芯到云巨头加速外售迭代，海外头部企业正从“买算力”转向“定义算力”，人工智能算力主权争夺已全面进入系统级竞争新阶段。

我国坚定推进“国芯训国模”战略，算力自主化成果密集落地。6月，DeepSeek完成首轮510亿元外部融资，聚焦国产算力扩建与自研芯片；美团开源万亿参数大模型LongCat-2.0（1.6万亿参数），全程依托超5万张国产算力卡完成训练与推理，为业界首个纯国产算力万亿级模型；华为昇腾384超节点提供300PFLOPS密集BF16算力，性能接近英伟达GB200 NVL72两倍，已用于训练盘古Ultra MoE大模型；粤港澳大湾区首个昇腾万卡智算集群在韶关上线，总算力达9000P；我国首颗采用软件定义与三维近存计算技术的AI芯片在上海发布，在14纳米制程上实现每秒520万亿次浮点运算。当前，国内大模型企业正稳步推进算力“换芯工程”，核心预训练算力加速从海外GPU向国产AI芯片迁移，自主可控产业闭环加速成型。

规则治理博弈 从技术领先走向规则主导

随着大模型战略价值持续凸显，全球博弈从产业技术层面上升至制度规则层面，治理规则制定权成为各国角力的核心焦点。2026年以来，主要经济体加速人工智能治理立法，单边规制与多边协同并行推进，全球大模型治理进入制度化、体系化新阶段。

技术出口管制成为治理博弈前沿。前沿大模型的核心价值凝结于模型权重体系，具备极强的战略稀缺性。美国将其纳入国家战略管控体系，GPT-5.6等前沿模型仅对政府审批的合规主体开放，人工智能技术正式具备战略物资属性。欧洲加快自主布局，法国在“法国2030”框架下追加6.55亿欧元人工智能投资，明确破除数字领域战略依赖；欧盟出台“欧洲技术主权一揽子方案”，通过《芯片法案2.0》和《云与人工智能发展法案》，加强欧洲在半导体、人工智能、云计算和开源等领域能力。全球AI竞争已升级为国家安全层面的战略博弈。

全球多边治理体系建设加速推进。7月，首届联合国人工智能治理全球对话在日内瓦召开，聚焦大模型虚假信息传播、就业替代、算法偏见等系统性跨国风险，倡导构建协同共治、公平包容的全球人工智能治理体系。同月，2026世界人工智能大会暨人工智能全球治理高级别会议在上海举办，中方系统阐释我国人工智能发展与治理的核心理念、政策主张，为全球AI向善发展、完善全球治理体系贡献中国方案，这是我国在全球人工智能治理领域发挥负责任大国作用的重要体现，也为推动构建人类命运共同体注入了新动力。

本土化治理规制形成差异化格局。各国依据自身产业基础与战略诉求选择不同治理路径，欧盟以全面立法构建风险分级监管体系，《人工智能法案》明确数据透明与能耗披露义务；美国以行政令构建自愿框架，6月出台《促进先进人工智能创新与安全》行政令，呈现“去监管化”与“安全回摆”双重特征；韩国《人工智能发展与建立信任基本法》于1月实施；新加坡2026年1月推出全球首个《智能体人工智能治理示范框架》，治理路径锚定于自愿性框架与行业指引；我国率先发布《全球人工智能治理倡议》，确立“智能向善、安全可控、普惠公平”治理导向，坚持“包容审慎、分类分级”监管原则，立法策略从2023年《生成式人工智能服务管理暂行办法》升级到2026年《智能体规范应用与创新发展实施意见》，监管范围从“大模型”延伸至“智能体”。截至2026年6月30日，累计有988款生成式人工智能服务完成备案，598款应用或功能完成登记。当前，全球AI治理呈现“欧盟全面立法、美国构建自愿框架、韩国顶层设计、新加坡柔性指引、中国包容普惠”的差异化格局。

review_queue.title: Two out of three companies use generative AI, but productivity is dragging its heels.
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: TIME France
Date: 2026-09-03T15:30:07+00:00
Source language: fr
Original headline: Deux entreprises sur trois utilisent l’IA générative, mais la productivité traîne des pieds
English normalization: Two out of three companies use generative AI, but productivity is dragging its heels.
Collected full article body: Dans le champ couvert par la Banque de France, deux entreprises d’au moins 20 salariés sur trois utilisent désormais l’intelligence artificielle générative. Début 2026, 67 % d’entre elles déclaraient déjà y avoir recours. Son usage est donc devenu majoritaire, même s’il demeure le plus souvent limité ou expérimental. Le chiffre, dévoilé par la Banque de France dans son bulletin publié ce 3 septembre, tranche avec les discours prophétiques sur la révolution imminente : l’IA s’est bel et bien installée dans les entreprises, mais elle n’a pas encore transformé l’économie française.

L’enquête, menée du 25 février au 3 avril 2026 auprès de quelque 7 000 entreprises, couvre l’industrie manufacturière, la construction et une large partie des services marchands, soit environ la moitié de l’économie française. Elle dessine une diffusion à deux vitesses. L’adoption reste inégale selon la taille des entreprises : 83 % de celles qui comptent au moins 1 000 salariés utilisent déjà l’IA générative, contre 64 % des entreprises de 20 à 49 salariés. L’IA générative, dont la barrière à l’entrée est relativement faible, s’impose largement. L’IA prédictive, plus exigeante en données et en capacités d’intégration, reste davantage concentrée dans les grandes structures.

Rédiger, résumer, classer : l’IA cantonnée aux tâches de bureau

Cet usage massif ne rime pas avec sophistication. Dans 74 % des entreprises utilisatrices, l’IA sert d’abord les fonctions support ou transversales, notamment les ventes, l’administration, la finance ou les ressources humaines. Seules 14 % déclarent l’utiliser en priorité dans leurs processus de production. La génération de texte domine très largement les usages, loin devant les outils plus complexes intégrés aux systèmes d’information. Chez les entreprises qui n’utilisent pas encore l’IA, le principal frein est d’ailleurs l’absence de cas d’usage identifié, loin devant le manque de compétences ou le coût. Deux secteurs se distinguent toutefois par leur avance, avec un usage particulièrement intensif : l’information-communication et les activités spécialisées, scientifiques et techniques.

Cette fracture se lit aussi fonction par fonction. L’étude Trends of AI menée par KPMG auprès de 356 décideurs, principalement issus de grands groupes et d’entreprises de taille intermédiaire, montre que le marketing reste le principal terrain d’adoption, notamment pour le résumé de conversations, la traduction et la génération de contenus. Dans les directions informatiques, la logique change : l’IA sert avant tout à fiabiliser les processus et à améliorer la productivité. La finance, elle, avance à pas comptés, en misant d’abord sur la formation et la gestion des connaissances avant de s’aventurer sur des tâches plus sensibles.

Seules 31 % des entreprises utilisatrices d’IA générative constatent un gain de productivité

Cette hétérogénéité se retrouve à l’échelle de la zone euro. Selon une note de la Banque centrale européenne, 52 % des personnes en emploi interrogées dans onze pays utilisent désormais l’IA au travail. L’utilisateur médian déclare gagner trois heures par semaine, soit 7,7 % de son temps de travail. Les gains les plus élevés concernent la programmation, l’analyse de données et l’automatisation des tâches répétitives. Ils sont beaucoup plus modestes pour la recherche d’informations ou la rédaction courante. Mais gagner du temps ne signifie pas nécessairement produire davantage : rapportées à l’ensemble des travailleurs, ces économies de temps correspondent à un gain d’efficacité agrégé estimé à 3,8 %. Celui-ci ne se traduit en hausse de la productivité que si le temps libéré permet de produire davantage. Les économistes António Dias da Silva, Laura Lebastard et David Sondermann, auteurs de la note, le reconnaissent :

« Des obstacles persistent tant du côté des travailleurs que des entreprises. »

Le pari reste à gagner

Sur le terrain, les effets restent en pointillé. Seules 31 % des entreprises utilisatrices d’IA générative constatent un gain de productivité, selon la Banque de France. Au cours des trois dernières années, l’effet observé sur l’emploi est resté modeste : en solde net, 2 % des entreprises utilisant l’IA générative et 3 % de celles recourant à l’IA prédictive lui attribuent une baisse de leurs effectifs. Ce que révèle surtout l’enquête, c’est la prudence des dirigeants : les entreprises constatent une hausse de leurs investissements liés à l’IA et, plus rarement, une augmentation de leurs prix de vente, mais pas d’économies massives à court terme.

L’avenir, en revanche, pourrait être plus tranché. Parmi les entreprises qui utilisent ou prévoient d’utiliser l’IA, 60 % anticipent un effet positif sur leur productivité d’ici 2029, dont 17 % un effet jugé significatif. Un cinquième d’entre elles envisagent aussi une réduction d’effectifs, modérée pour la plupart, tandis qu’un tiers prévoit une hausse de ses investissements. La phase d’expérimentation est donc loin d’être achevée, mais les entreprises envisagent déjà des déploiements plus structurés. La Banque de France résume ainsi l’enjeu :

« L’enjeu économique réside désormais moins dans l’adoption de l’IA que dans sa capacité à transformer durablement l’organisation et la performance des entreprises. »

Events

Applications of Artificial Intelligence in the Use of ICD-11 for Morbidity and Mortality

Copied to clipboard

Applications of Artificial Intelligence in the Use of ICD-11 for Morbidity and Mortality

September 10, 2026

11:00 a.m. (Eastern Time)

Simultaneous interpretation in English, Spanish, Portuguese, and French.

REGISTER HERE

Artificial Intelligence offers new possibilities for supporting the use of clinical information in morbidity and mortality processes based on international standards such as the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11).

During this session,

Daniel Luna

,

Charly Otero

, and

Juan Carlos Díaz

will present Artificial Intelligence applications that use available clinical information—such as a discharge or hospitalization summary—to identify relevant conditions and assist, as appropriate, in determining the main condition and developing a proposed cause-of-death sequence.

These tools can also suggest ICD-10 or ICD-11 codes, facilitate the review of their correspondence, and enable users to consult alternative terminology. The resulting proposals must be reviewed, modified when necessary, and validated by the responsible health professional.

The session will focus on using clinical information to support these processes and assist with cause-of-death certification. This process should be distinguished from the subsequent statistical coding and selection of the Underlying Cause of Death, which is conducted by applying the World Health Organization’s mortality coding and selection rules.

The speakers will also discuss the benefits and limitations of these applications, as well as considerations related to information quality, interoperability, semantic standards, ethics, data governance, transparency, and human oversight. Artificial Intelligence is presented as a support tool and does not replace clinical judgment or the responsibility of the certifying physician.

This event is being held within the framework of the Community of Practice on Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) in Latin America and the Caribbean. It is part of the thematic area on the digital transformation of CRVS, which seeks to promote the active exchange of good practices and relevant information to strengthen these systems throughout the Region.

Objectives

Overall objective of the series:

To strengthen technical and institutional capacities to use ICD-11 as a central semantic standard in Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) and Information Systems for Health (IS4H), improving the quality and integration of morbidity and mortality data and enabling the interoperability required for digital transformation in health and informed decision-making.

Specific objective of the session:

To explore applications of Artificial Intelligence in the use of ICD-11 for morbidity and mortality, particularly for analyzing clinical information, identifying relevant conditions, supporting the determination of the main condition, and assisting in the development of a proposed cause-of-death sequence, always subject to review and validation by the responsible health professional.

Speakers

Daniel Luna

Physician with master’s and doctoral degrees in Computer Science and extensive experience in health informatics. He led the development of the clinical information system at Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires and currently heads its Department of Health Informatics.

Charly Otero

Physician with a master’s degree in Biomedical Informatics and more than 20 years of experience in digital health, interoperability, and information systems. He has led projects and advised health institutions and government agencies throughout Latin America.

Juan Carlos Díaz

Data Engineering Advisor at the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), specializing in transforming complex data into actionable insights to support decision-making. He promotes the creative and responsible use of data and Artificial Intelligence in public health.

Moderator:

Myrna Martí

, IS4H Advisor and Digital Literacy Program Coordinator at the Pan American Health Organization.

Artificial intelligence is a tool that informs the professional activity of New York attorneys. AI is embedded in legal research platforms, case management tools, and e-discovery systems. Yet the adoption of these tools has outpaced practitioners' understanding of their limitations and risks, particularly with respect to bias, equity, and professional responsibility.

This CLE program, the first of a series, equips New York attorneys with a practical, rigorous foundation for navigating AI in legal practice. Drawing on the findings of the New York Judiciary's Bias and Equity Subcommittee of the Advisory Committee on AI & the Courts, and leading scholarship on AI bias in the legal industry, the curriculum addresses both the systemic challenges AI poses to equal justice and the specific professional responsibility obligations attorneys must satisfy when deploying these tools.

Collected full article body: The University of Michigan called for community input regarding a set of proposals for how to handle generative artificial intelligence on campus Thursday. The recommendations come from the AI in Education Working Group, which was established in December 2025 to investigate the role of AI in classrooms and provide policy suggestions. Feedback will be accepted through a community comment form until Sept. 17.

The group’s objective was to offer strategic suggestions to the University based on faculty feedback, student surveys and a benchmarking study of AI approaches at other universities. In a report, the group outlined the challenges with AI and education.

“AI systems have been developed to speed up processes; learning requires processes that slow things down,” the report read. “To learn is to confront desirable difficulties and overcome them through productive struggle. … But it is in education that AI’s fundamental purpose to make things easier and faster poses a particular challenge.”

The report made various policy recommendations, including establishing AI literacy training for students and faculty, creating an AI advisory board, setting up AI-free spaces for learning and avoiding AI-based surveillance. It also suggested taking different approaches to AI depending on the setting; it proposed that committees from different curriculums would decide specific policies that vary by school or program.

“The working group recommends that the University of Michigan approach generative AI through a spirit of deliberate experimentation, piloting diverse strategies, learning from what works, and scaling investment thoughtfully as evidence emerges,” the report read. “This iterative approach reflects U-M’s commitment to rigorous inquiry applied to its own institutional practices.”

Gregory Teachout, director of communications and strategic initiatives in the Office of the Provost, wrote in a Sept. 3 University Record article that the University plans to collect community feedback about and to inform future University policies.

“The principles also state that people, rather than AI systems, retain final responsibility for the decisions and outcomes associated with their use of AI,” Teachout wrote. “Several implementation steps reflecting the principles and recommendations from the AI in Education Working Group report will begin during the 2026-27 academic year.”

Teachout also wrote there will be school-specific adoptions of AI and experimental AI-competency programs throughout the upcoming academic year.

“During the 2026-27 academic year, 20 courses will carry out pilot explorations to evaluate the integration of AI into a range of aspects of curricular activity,” Teachout wrote. “The pilots will provide opportunities to examine different approaches to AI-supported teaching and learning and build practical experience as schools and colleges develop their longer-term plans.”

La solution, discrètement à l’essai depuis plusieurs mois et développée par une jeune pousse montréalaise, suscite des critiques.

Depuis janvier, les bandes vidéo des caméras de surveillance des stations Papineau et Place-Saint-Henri sont analysées par l’intelligence artificielle, dans le cadre d’un projet pilote. La preuve de concept, élaborée par la firme Lipslogics, permet d’identifier les flâneurs lorsque vient le temps de fermer les stations de métro, à la tombée de la nuit.

Par exemple, lorsqu'un individu est détecté dans une station une heure avant sa fermeture, une notification est envoyée à la centrale de répartition de visio opérationnelle, qui avise par la suite les constables spéciaux afin qu'ils puissent le guider vers la sortie. L'objectif est d'accélérer la fermeture des stations pendant la nuit, durant laquelle se déroulent des travaux d'entretien.

Les signalements seront toujours validés au préalable par un humain avant d'être transmis aux constables spéciaux, précise la STM. (Photo d'archives)

Photo : Radio-Canada

On est vraiment très primitif en termes de ce qu'on veut faire. C'est vraiment [pour détecter] une présence humaine dans une heure donnée et une station donnée

, assure le chef de division en sûreté corporative à la STM, Zakaria Hajji. La solution n'est pas associée à une base de données permettant d’identifier les personnes

et les bandes vidéo sont détruites après 5 à 10 jours, ajoute la Société de transport de Montréal.

Rectificatif

Dans la version originale de ce texte, la STM avait déclaré par erreur que les images étaient conservées pendant 72 heures. La société de transport précise que les bandes vidéos des caméras en stations sont plutôt conservées sur une période de 5 à 10 jours. Ces temps standards n’ont pas changé dans le cadre du projet pilote

.

La technologie pourrait être implantée dans quatre stations supplémentaires d’ici la fin de son élaboration, prévue en avril. Ensuite, la STM évaluera si la solution d’IA peut générer des gains opérationnels qui justifieraient un investissement

. Cette collaboration s'est faite sans coût pour la Société, mais elle a dû octroyer un contrat de gré à gré de 103 477 $ à la firme le mois dernier pour poursuivre le développement de la solution.

Justifié?

La Ligue des droits et libertés (LDL), qui surveille le déploiement de ce genre de technologie, croit que l'usage de l'IA pour détecter les flâneurs dans le métro va trop loin.

La surveillance à des fins de gestion, ce n'est pas un motif qui justifie ce genre de surveillance

, affirme Dominique Peschard, membre du comité Surveillance des populations, intelligence artificielle et droits humains pour la LDL.

Qu’est-ce qui va empêcher le logiciel d’être utilisé à d’autres moments que la fermeture simplement pour expulser des itinérants du métro?

s'interroge M. Peschard.

Il y a des nuits, en toute transparence, [où] on n’arrive même pas à faire tous les raccompagnements [avant] que les stations soient en train de rouvrir.

Un manque de transparence dénoncé

La preuve de concept est à l'essai depuis le début de l'année, mais n'a fait l'objet d'aucune annonce publique de la part de la STM. Une erreur, selon Sébastien Gambs, professeur d'informatique à l'Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM).

Ce qui serait important d'abord, c’est la transparence. D'avertir les gens quand ils rentrent dans ces stations-là, de leur dire qu’au-delà des caméras classiques de surveillance, on teste un nouveau système

, cite en exemple celui qui est aussi titulaire de la Chaire de recherche du Canada en analyse respectueuse de la vie privée et éthique des données massives.

Sébastien Gambs est professeur d'informatique à l'UQAM et titulaire de la Chaire de recherche du Canada en analyse respectueuse de la vie privée et éthique des données massives.

Photo : Radio-Canada / Édouard Beaudoin

Sébastien Gambs se questionne également sur l'accès aux données colligées par la solution. Par écrit, la STM assure qu'elles ne circulent que sur ses serveurs. Le fait qu’elles soient stockées localement, c’est bien, mais la question c’est : qui a accès à ces données-là pendant les 72 heures?

se demande le professeur à l'UQAM.

Les données sont actuellement à la disposition des employés de la firme parce qu'ils doivent faire des tests

Tant la Ligue des droits et libertés que le professeur Gambs s'inquiètent des biais algorithmiques que pourrait générer la solution d'IA. Une crainte que partage aussi le Réseau Solidarité Itinérance Québec, qui appréhende que certaines personnes fassent davantage l'objet de signalements que d'autres.

Est-ce qu’il y a une équité? Si quelqu’un d’un peu sale avec une tuque est assis, est-ce qu'on y va? Alors que si c’est un monsieur en veston qui parle au téléphone et qui traîne dans un coin avec exactement le même comportement, est-ce qu'on va lui laisser une chance?

Aucun nouveau dispositif physique n'a été nécessaire pour élaborer cette preuve de concept, selon la STM.

Photo : Radio-Canada / Martin Hazel

La STM réitère que son objectif est strictement d'optimiser ses opérations. Peu importe votre race, votre couleur, votre poids, votre coupe de cheveux, ce n'est pas important pour nous. C'est vraiment cette présence humaine dans les installations qui compte aujourd'hui

, rassure M. Hajji.

La firme qui conçoit la solution n'a pas répondu à nos questions. Notre mission est d’accroître la productivité des entreprises à l’échelle mondiale grâce à la recherche opérationnelle et aux systèmes de décision intelligents, tout en offrant des transformations complètes

, peut-on lire sur le site web de Lipslogics.
